note: The Aragonese jota first: Zaragoza cantadores with their rondallas on 78s and in Alan Lomax's 1952 recordings, then the jotas of Castile, Valencia, Mallorca, Galicia and the Basque Country, and the folk revival from the 1970s to today. Lomax's tracks were recorded in 1952 and issued on CD much later, so their years are left open.

size.basis: Aragon alone: the Fonoteca de la Jota in the Biblioteca de Aragón holds over 2,000 audio recordings (es.wikipedia); José Oto alone made about fifty discs; 78s by Miguel Asso, Jacinta Bartolomé, Pilar Gascón and others fill about three pages of the jota genre listing at UCLA's Strachwitz Frontera Collection; Jesús Gracia and the Pastor de Andorra recorded LPs from the 1950s to the 1990s. Beyond Aragon every Spanish region has its own jota, recorded in field anthologies (Lomax 1952, La tradición musical en España) and by revival groups since the 1970s (La Bullonera, Al Tall, Candeal, Hadit, La Musgaña, Eliseo Parra), each album carrying several jotas; MusicBrainz lists about 1,100 recordings with jota in the title, a fraction of the whole. Range is a reasoned guess, not a catalogue count; core is what an Aragonese listener would call essential, plus the main regional and revival recordings.
